extracted.intended_audience: PhD candidates (esp. social sciences), supervisors, researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and writing the introduction chapter of a PhD thesis, including problem statements, research questions, hypotheses, contributions, and presentation/style recommendations. Aimed at helping doctoral candidates produce a scientifically valid, well-organised introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult your supervisors
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult your supervisors or your department about the format of your thesis before starting to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions vary in thesis requirements; check local/departmental expectations first. Early consultation avoids format/style mismatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarize yourself with the style or format of thesis writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the required thesis style or format (institutional conventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand chapter structure, referencing and other formatting rules to ensure compliance with institutional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide on the word length
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how many words your thesis should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow institutional/departmental word limits and plan content accordingly; being concise helps reader comprehension even if introduction has no strict word limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn referencing styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn more about referencing styles and make sure you have necessary information for the reference section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect full bibliographic data early; maintain consistent citation formatting (e.g., APA, MLA). Poor referencing undermines scholarly credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn about indexing of your thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand indexing requirements for the thesis (e.g., table of contents, lists of figures/tables, keywords).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan indexing and front/back matter so readers and examiners can navigate your thesis easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the problem or phenomenon to be investigated
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly state the central problem or phenomenon your research will investigate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This should be presented early in the introduction and motivate the entire thesis; link to evidence and literature that shows it is a serious, research-worthy problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the party affected by the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify who is affected by the problem under investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify stakeholders, populations, or contexts impacted to show relevance and practical importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how you plan to solve the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the approach or plan for addressing the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concise roadmap of methods, analytical approach, or theoretical angle that will be used to address the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convince the reader you are qualified
rubrics_metrics.description: Convince the reader that you are qualified and equipped with appropriate methods to solve the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate competence via literature grounding, methodological rigor, and rationale for chosen approach; this builds examiner confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight benefits of solving the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the benefits or significance of solving the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State practical, theoretical, cultural, economic or societal payoffs; relate benefits to gaps in the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the reader anticipated results
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reader what results you anticipate (if appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anticipated outcomes to indicate direction and impact, but avoid overstating certainty; relate to hypotheses where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate the rationale of your research
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the importance and rationale of your research clearly and early in the introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with general statements then narrow to the research problem, questions, objectives and hypotheses; be motivating, concise and engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise and clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Write clearly, precisely and concisely in the introduction to help readers comprehend major issues quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although there may be no strict word limit, concision aids comprehension; avoid unnecessary detail in the introduction and reserve depth for later chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organise introduction as a preview/roadmap
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare the introduction as a preview so readers can judge the rest of your work and its significance at a glance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include problem statement, objectives, hypothesis, methods summary, and anticipated contributions; make structure explicit to guide readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep best for last / write introduction after finishing thesis if possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If possible, write the introduction once everything else is finished to avoid missing important elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completing other chapters first helps ensure the introduction accurately represents the thesis' final scope and contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of introductions (use appropriate opening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an opening style suited to your topic: Illusion, Analogue, Narrative, Descriptive, Definition, Example, Question, Statistic, or Quotation introductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an opening that captures attention and fits disciplinary conventions; e.g., statistic introductions suit empirically grounded problems, narrative may fit qualitative work. Avoid gimmicks incompatible with academic tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis (introduction) statement criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Your thesis statement must declare your topic and assert how you will prove/disprove the problem; make an assertion about your interpretation and capture reader attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the statement challenges peers, anticipates readers' expectations, and organizes existing evidence clearly and logically; avoid arguing facts without evidence—use scholarly sources to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem statement concise form
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem statement should state a specific condition that needs urgent attention and typically be a line or two with elaboration following.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe why the issue merits investigation, cite scholarly references, and show how your study fills or narrows a gap in the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem statement must answer key questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A PhD problem statement should seek to answer: What is the problem? Where is it? How can it be solved? Why solve it? Is it current? Will it persist if not solved? Who is affected? Will it prove/disprove existing knowledge?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these eight guiding questions to shape a focused, researchable problem statement and to justify significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of the problem statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem statement: highlights importance, creates interest, adds new knowledge, identifies literature gaps, indicates need for future research, and stimulates further thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly articulate these impacts to persuade examiners and readers of the significance of your research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’ts when writing a problem statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid selecting problems that are un-researchable, unsupported by scholarly documents, beyond your qualifications/resources, or lacking practical benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess feasibility, literature base, your competency, and practical significance before committing to a problem; these are common anti-patterns that waste time and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for a research problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a research problem based on: personal interest, background knowledge, conceptual/theoretical soundness, and data availability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interest ensures motivation; prior study provides authority; conceptual soundness grounds inquiry; data availability ensures feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research question centrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Research questions focus the study, regulate methodology, and guide investigation, analysis, and answering the problem statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good research question is deeper than the topic, removes ambiguity, and aligns with appropriate methods and data collection strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing effective research questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a thought-provoking topic of interest supported by scholarly literature; questions should require critical analysis and not be answerable by simple facts; avoid too broad or too narrow scopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vet research questions with your supervisor; ensure they guide the type of investigation and identify needed data and analytical approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of research questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Research questions can be descriptive, explanatory (why), hypothetical/predictive, open-ended, or closed-ended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match question type to method: closed questions fit quantitative measures; open-ended suit qualitative inquiry; explanatory questions often require causal designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons researchers ask questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions guide finding answers, help focus the topic, concentrate on important issues, and assist in testing hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use questions actively to structure literature review, methodology, and analysis so each stage contributes to answering them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis is an unproven reasoning or educated guess predicting relationships or results under specific conditions; it requires rigorous testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses are optional in some studies but useful to direct testing; they become scientific knowledge only after appropriate validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a good hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis should be simple, relevant to the study, testable in the field, verifiable, and realistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a hypothesis lacks these traits outcomes will not be desirable; ensure operational definitions and measurable constructs to enable testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why hypotheses are needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses validate research activity, determine truth of assumptions, direct inquiry, save time/resources, help collect relevant data, lead to meaningful conclusions, focus issues, assist data collection, and may strengthen theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hypotheses to structure sampling, measurement and statistical testing; do not create hypotheses that cannot be empirically evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common hypothesis types (Null and Alternative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Null Hypothesis (H0): assumes no difference/effect. Alternative Hypothesis (H1): assumes a difference/effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate clear, testable null and alternative hypotheses suited to statistical testing; examples provided for group comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to test hypotheses (practical steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps: choose hypothesis type, determine sample size, collect data, determine significance level, compute P-value, decide to accept or reject hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow established statistical procedures; ensure sampling and analysis choices match the hypotheses and research design to avoid invalid inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common errors in hypothesis testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors can arise from poor research design, inadequate population/sampling, questionable data analysis/statistics, or incorrect conclusions. Two statistical errors: Type I (reject true null) and Type II (accept false null).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan research design and sampling carefully; choose appropriate statistical tests and report limitations; discuss both types of errors in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution criteria for a PhD thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: PhD research should make specific, focused contributions to knowledge — e.g., explain importance of problem, present findings, transform existing theory, discuss generalizability and added value (economic, cultural, societal), demonstrate experimental/empirical significance, highlight research area's relevance, and/or contribute novel methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List concrete contributions with evidence; measure significance objectively where possible (e.g., empirical confirmation, scope of applicability, methodological innovation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of significance (seven ways)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seven ways to measure significance: 1) explain importance of the research problem, 2) your findings, 3) transformation of existing theory, 4) generalizability/added values (economic/cultural/societal, scope/scale), 5) experimental significance (empirical confirmation), 6) research area relevance, 7) research method novelty and creativity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these dimensions to justify the claim of 'significance' rather than treating it as purely subjective; provide evidence under each applicable dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution must be verifiable and original
rubrics_metrics.description: For a PhD contribution to be valid it must be genuine, original, verifiable, re-do-able and challengeable by other researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies so that others can replicate or critically evaluate your methods and results; clearly state novelty versus extension of previous work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of Knowledge (B.O.K.) entry criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To be recognized as part of the professional 'body of knowledge', a PhD must add new knowledge into the existing system so the author can be considered a professional member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame contributions in relation to existing B.O.K. and demonstrate how the thesis advances that collective system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples/evidence to demonstrate contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Show there is insufficient investigation on your topic, empirical disputes, or how your work proves/disproves prior findings; provide empirical confirmation and concrete impact evidence (where/whom/how).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical data, replication, or methodological novelty to substantiate claims of contribution; anticipate possible challenges and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis as a scientific and scholarly document
rubrics_metrics.description: A PhD thesis should be scientific and scholarly, containing researched material, experimentations, contributions and findings that can solve or mitigate a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standardized global thesis format; include a proposal that clearly states What, Why, How, and When. Emphasize scientific rigor in design, methods and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal as first crucial stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Your proposal is the first stage and must correctly state the What, Why, How, and When of your thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the proposal to plan feasibility, methodology, timeline, and to secure supervisor approval; a clear proposal prevents scope creep and design flaws.
